claim: RecA orchestrates the cellular response to DNA damage via its multiple roles in the bacterial SOS response.
source: The RecA protein orchestrates the cellular response to DNA damage via its multiple roles in the bacterial SOS response.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general characterization of RecA function.

claim: RecA is largely sequestered in storage structures during normal metabolism.
source: Single-molecule imaging techniques in live cells demonstrate that RecA is largely sequestered in storage structures during normal metabolism.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon DNA damage, the storage structures dissolve and the cytosolic pool of RecA rapidly nucleates to form early SOS-signaling complexes.
source: Upon DNA damage, the storage structures dissolve and the cytosolic pool of RecA rapidly nucleates to form early SOS-signaling complexes, maturing into DNA-bound RecA bundles at later time points.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: RecA* largely appears at locations distal from replisomes both before and after SOS induction.
source: Both before and after SOS induction, RecA* largely appears at locations distal from replisomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by co-localization experiments.

claim: Upon completion of repair, RecA storage structures reform.
source: Upon completion of repair, RecA storage structures reform.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by time-lapse imaging data.

claim: RecA* catalyzes auto-proteolysis of the transcriptional repressor LexA to induce expression of more than 40 SOS genes.
source: RecA* catalyzes auto-proteolysis of the transcriptional repressor LexA to induce expression of more than 40 SOS genes (Courcelle et al., 2001; Fernández De Henestrosa et al., 2000; Kenyon and Walker, 1980; Little and Mount, 1982; Little et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: RecA* uses the ssDNA generated when replication forks encounter DNA lesions as an induction signal.
source: RecA* thus uses the ssDNA generated when replication forks encounter DNA lesions as an induction signal (Sassanfar and Roberts, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RecA mediates error-free recombinational DNA repair at sites of single-strand gaps, double-strand breaks (DSBs) and failed replisomes.
source: Second, along with several other accessory proteins, RecA mediates error-free recombinational DNA repair at sites of single-strand gaps, double-strand breaks (DSBs) and failed replisomes (Cox et al., 2000; Kowalczykowski, 2000; Kuzminov, 1995; Lusetti and Cox, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The formation and activity of active DNA Polymerase V complex capable of lesion bypass requires RecA*.
source: Third, the formation and activity of active DNA Polymerase V complex capable of lesion bypass requires RecA* (Jaszczur et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2009; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: RecA is a prototypical member of a class of proteins that are critical for genomic stability across all domains of life.
source: RecA is a prototypical member of a class of proteins that are critical for genomic stability across all domains of life (Baumann et al., 1996; Bianco et al., 1998; Lusetti et al., 2003b; San Filippo et al., 2008; Sung, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In higher organisms, including humans, the homologous protein Rad51 supports error-free double-strand break repair by catalyzing strand exchange much like the RecA protein does in eubacteria.
source: In higher organisms, including humans, the homologous protein Rad51 supports error-free double-strand break repair by catalyzing strand exchange much like the RecA protein does in eubacteria (Baumann et al., 1996; Sung, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in human Rad51 and accessory proteins have been implicated in carcinomas and Fanconi anemia.
source: Mutations in human Rad51 and accessory proteins have been implicated in carcinomas and Fanconi anemia (Chen et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2000; Prakash et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transcription of the recA gene is upregulated ten-fold within minutes after DNA damage.
source: In response to DNA damage, transcription of the recA gene is upregulated ten-fold within minutes (Courcelle et al., 2001; Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The copy number of RecA in undamaged cells has been estimated to be about 7000–15,000 per cell, increasing to 100,000 per cell upon triggering the DNA-damage response.
source: Using immunostaining, the copy number of RecA in undamaged cells has been estimated to be about 7000–15,000 per cell, increasing to 100,000 per cell upon triggering the DNA-damage response (Boudsocq et al., 1997; Stohl et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RecA forms foci in cells.
source: Visualization of C-terminal GFP fusions of wild-type and mutant recA alleles placed under the native recA promoter in E. coli have revealed that RecA forms foci in cells (Lesterlin et al., 2014; Renzette et al., 2005; Renzette et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RecA fusions to fluorescent proteins have consistently resulted in proteins with reduced function.
source: (1) RecA fusions to fluorescent proteins have consistently resulted in proteins with reduced function (Handa et al., 2009; Renzette et al., 2005), making interpretation of the localizations revealed by these tagged proteins highly challenging.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fluorescent proteins do not behave as inert tags and can influence intracellular localization in bacterial cells.
source: (2) This issue is further complicated by the fact that fluorescent proteins do not behave as inert tags and can influence intracellular localization in bacterial cells (Ghodke et al., 2016; Ouzounov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bacillus subtilis RecA tagged with GFP, YFP and mRFP yielded different localizations in response to DNA damage.
source: Indeed, Bacillus subtilis RecA tagged with GFP, YFP and mRFP yielded different localizations in response to DNA damage (Kidane and Graumann, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both N- and C-terminal ends are important for RecA function and localization.
source: These challenges do not come as a surprise since both N- and C-terminal ends are important for RecA function and localization (Eggler et al., 2003; Lusetti et al., 2003b; Lusetti et al., 2003a; Rajendram et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Untagged RecA has a remarkable ability to self-assemble into different complexes that form on single-stranded DNA (RecA*), on double-stranded DNA, or are free of DNA.
source: (3) At least in vitro, untagged RecA has a remarkable ability to self-assemble, into different complexes that form on single-stranded DNA (RecA*), on double-stranded DNA, or are free of DNA (Brenner et al., 1988; Egelman and Stasiak, 1986, Egelman and Stasiak, 1988; Stasiak and Egelman, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the absence of DNA, RecA can polymerize to form aggregates of various stoichiometry to yield dimers, tetramers, 'rods' and 'bundles'.
source: In the absence of DNA, RecA can polymerize to form aggregates of various stoichiometry to yield dimers, tetramers, 'rods' and 'bundles' (Brenner et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RecA fusions with the best functionality have revealed DNA-free aggregates that are confined to the cellular poles, outside of the nucleoid and associated with anionic phospholipids in the inner membrane.
source: Some of these states may have a physiological relevance: RecA fusions with the best functionality have revealed DNA-free aggregates that are confined to the cellular poles, outside of the nucleoid and associated with anionic phospholipids in the inner membrane (Rajendram et al., 2015; Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple dsDNA-RecA-ATPγS filaments can associate to form structures termed as 'bundles'.
source: Early electron-microscopy (EM) studies revealed that multiple dsDNA-RecA-ATPγS filaments could also associate to form structures confusingly termed as 'bundles' (Egelman and Stasiak, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: ssDNA-RecA-ATPγS filaments can aggregate together.
source: This study also identified that ssDNA-RecA-ATPγS filaments could aggregate together.
evidence: This refers to the Egelman and Stasiak, 1988 study mentioned in the previous sentence.

claim: Electron microscopy of cells revealed that RecA appeared to form 'bundles' that were aligned next to the inner membrane in cells after DNA damage.
source: Electron microscopy of cells revealed that RecA appeared to form 'bundles' that were aligned next to the inner membrane in cells after DNA damage (Levin-Zaidman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In cells carrying an additional allele of wild-type RecA at a secondary chromosomal locus to increase overall RecA function, long RecA structures called 'bundles' were formed during double-strand break repair.
source: In cells carrying an additional allele of wild-type RecA at a secondary chromosomal locus to increase overall RecA function, long RecA structures called 'bundles' were formed during double-strand break repair (Lesterlin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RecA bundles form after SOS induction by other means than double-strand breaks, and also then interact with anionic phospholipids in the inner membrane.
source: RecA bundles form after SOS induction by other means than double-strand breaks, and also then interact with anionic phospholipids in the inner membrane (Garvey et al., 1985; Rajendram et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A monomeric C-terminal fragment of the λ repressor (mCI) was developed as a novel fluorescent probe that specifically interacts with RecA filaments on single-stranded DNA (RecA*).
source: Here, we develop a monomeric C-terminal fragment of the λ repressor as a novel fluorescent probe that specifically interacts with RecA filaments on single-stranded DNA (RecA*).
evidence: This is a primary methodological development stated in the abstract.

claim: The bacteriophage λ repressor CI exhibits RecA*-dependent auto-proteolysis in response to DNA damage.
source: In response to DNA damage, the λ repressor CI exhibits RecA*-dependent auto-proteolysis, much like the homologous proteins in bacteria, LexA and UmuD (Burckhardt et al., 1988; Ferentz et al., 1997; Luo et al., 2001; Roberts and Roberts, 1975; Stayrook et al., 2008; Walker, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The ssDNA-RecA filament (RecA*) stabilizes a proteolysis-competent conformation of CI enabling auto-proteolysis at Ala111-Gly112.
source: In this reaction, the ssDNA-RecA filament (RecA*) stabilizes a proteolysis-competent conformation of CI enabling auto-proteolysis at Ala111-Gly112 (Ndjonka and Bell, 2006; Sauer et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The N-terminal DNA-binding domain of CI is dispensable for interactions with RecA*.
source: The N-terminal DNA-binding domain of CI is dispensable for interactions with RecA*(Gimble and Sauer, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A minimal C-terminal fragment of the λ repressor CI(101–229, A152T, P158T, K192A) efficiently inhibits the auto-catalytic cleavage of a hyper-cleavable monomeric C-terminal fragment CI(92-229).
source: A minimal C-terminal fragment of the λ repressor CI(101–229, A152T, P158T, K192A) (henceforth referred to as mCI, Molecular weight 14307.23 Da; Figure 1F) efficiently inhibits the auto-catalytic cleavage of a hyper-cleavable monomeric C-terminal fragment CI(92-229) (Ndjonka and Bell, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy has revealed that the mCI binds deep in the groove of the RecA filament.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy has revealed that the mCI binds deep in the groove of the RecA filament (Galkin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: mCI associates with the RecA filament in a biphasic manner.
source: These sensorgrams reveal that mCI associates with the RecA filament in a biphasic manner.
evidence: This is based on SPR experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Dissociation of mCI from the RecA filament was slow, with a dissociation halftime (t1/2) of 850 s.
source: Dissociation of mCI from the RecA filament was slow, with a dissociation halftime (t1/2) of 850 s.
evidence: This is based on SPR experimental data.

claim: YPet-mCI dissociated from RecA filaments with a t1/2 = 260 s.
source: We measured a t1/2 = 260 s and 280 s for YPet-mCI and PAmCherry-mCI respectively.
evidence: This is based on SPR experimental data.

claim: PAmCherry-mCI dissociated from RecA filaments with a t1/2 = 280 s.
source: We measured a t1/2 = 260 s and 280 s for YPet-mCI and PAmCherry-mCI respectively.
evidence: This is based on SPR experimental data.

claim: mCI binding to ssDNA-RecA filaments exhibits an equilibrium dissociation constant of 36 ± 10 nM with a Hill coefficient of 2.4 ± 0.2.
source: Fitting these data to the Hill equation yielded an equilibrium dissociation constant of 36 ± 10 nM with a Hill coefficient of 2.4 ± 0.2 (Figure 2J; error bars represent fitting errors).
evidence: This is based on smFRET experimental data.

claim: At high concentrations (5–10 μM), mCI can inhibit ATP hydrolysis and strand-exchange by RecA*, and delay LexA cleavage.
source: At high concentrations (5–10 μM), mCI can inhibit ATP hydrolysis and strand-exchange by RecA*, and delay LexA cleavage.
evidence: This is based on in vitro biochemical assays presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: At low concentrations (10–100 nM), key activities of RecA* are not significantly affected by the presence of mCI or tagged variant.
source: Importantly, at low concentrations (10–100 nM) similar to those we eventually employed as a standard in vivo (as described below), these key activities of RecA* are not significantly affected by the presence of mCI or tagged variant.
evidence: This is based on in vitro biochemical assays presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: mCI inhibits SOS induction in a concentration-dependent manner in cells.
source: Time-lapse acquisition after UV irradiation revealed that SOS induction was sensitive to the presence of mCI. Even leaky expression of mCI caused a measurable delay in GFP fluorescence (Figure 3A). This delay was found to be proportional to the expression level of mCI, and cells grown in 10−2% L-arabinose exhibited nearly complete inhibition of SOS induction during the experimental timeline of three hours after UV irradiation (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is based on live-cell imaging experiments measuring SOS reporter fluorescence.

claim: 20% of wild-type cells exhibited RecA* foci during normal growth.
source: Surprisingly, 20% of wild-type cells exhibited RecA* foci during normal growth.
evidence: This is based on live-cell PALM imaging of PAmCherry-mCI.

claim: Only 24% of RecA* foci detected during normal growth co-localized with replisomes.
source: However, only 24% of these co-localized with replisomes.
evidence: This is based on co-localization analysis of PAmCherry-mCI and ϵ-YPet foci.

claim: Upon exposure to ultraviolet light, 56% of cells exhibited RecA* foci.
source: Upon exposure to ultraviolet light, 56% of cells exhibited RecA* foci that were visualized by mCI, with up to 35% of the RecA* foci co-localized with replisomes at 60 min in rich media (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on live-cell PALM imaging and co-localization analysis.

claim: Up to 35% of the RecA* foci co-localized with replisomes at 60 min after UV in rich media.
source: Upon exposure to ultraviolet light, 56% of cells exhibited RecA* foci that were visualized by mCI, with up to 35% of the RecA* foci co-localized with replisomes at 60 min in rich media (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on live-cell PALM imaging and co-localization analysis.

claim: RecA bundles consist of RecA in a conformation that resembles that of RecA*.
source: Taken together these data suggest that RecA bundles consist of RecA in a conformation that resembles that of RecA*.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mCI stains RecA bundles and that bundle formation requires wild-type RecA.

claim: RecA forms DNA-free aggregates in vitro.
source: RecA forms DNA-free aggregates in vitro, and the R28A mutant of RecA exhibits fewer foci in cells when tagged to GFP (Eldin et al., 2000; Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The size of RecA storage structures is determined by the amount of cellular RecA.
source: Comparison of the Feret diameters of features in recA-gfp cells carrying the pConst-recA and pG353C-recA vectors revealed a strong dependence on the expression level of untagged wild-type RecA protein (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy measurements of RecA-GFP storage structures in cells with different RecA expression levels.

claim: Excess RecA is stored in the form of membrane-associated, phase separated, storage structures even in cells carrying untagged, wild-type RecA.
source: These results support the conclusion that excess RecA is stored in the form of membrane-associated, phase separated, storage structures even in cells carrying untagged, wild-type RecA.
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy images of cells stained with immunogold-labeled anti-RecA antibody.

claim: Storage structures dissolve within one hour after introducing damage.
source: We found that the storage structures dissolve within one hour after introducing damage, flooding the cell with RecA-GFP (Figure 6G, t = 1 hr).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging of recA-gfp/pG353C-recA cells after UV irradiation.

claim: For recA-gfp/pG353C-recA cells, half of the storage structures were lost within 45 ± 5 min after UV damage.
source: We found that for recA-gfp/pG353C-recA cells, half of the storage structures were lost within 45 ± 5 min after UV damage (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data.

claim: In recA-gfp/pG353C-recA cells, half of the population of storage structures that formed after UV damage did so after 135 ± 5 min after UV.
source: We then plotted the cumulative probability distribution of time of appearance of storage structures after SOS induction (Figure 6H, green curve). In these cells, half of the population of storage structures that formed after UV damage, did so after 135 ± 5 min after UV.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data.

claim: YPet-mCI was found to be cytosolic in the absence of DNA damage, suggesting a lack of stable association with RecA storage structures.
source: YPet-mCI was found to be cytosolic in the absence of DNA damage, suggesting a lack of stable association with RecA storage structures (Figure 6I, 'No UV' time point).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging of cells expressing YPet-mCI and pG353C-recA.

claim: Half of all bundles in recA-gfp cells appear by 60 min after UV.
source: Plotting a cumulative probability distribution of time of incidence of bundle formation revealed that half of all bundles in recA-gfp cells appear by 60 min after UV (Figure 6H, red curve).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of time-lapse imaging data.

claim: DinI promotes the formation of storage structures in cells.
source: In the absence of DNA damage, we detected storage structures in fewer ΔdinI cells (27% of 702 cells) compared to dinI+ cells (43% of 855 cells) (see Figure 6J).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging comparing dinI+ and ΔdinI cells.

claim: Over-expression of DinI from pBAD-dinI in ΔdinI cells recovered storage structures in the presence of L-arabinose.
source: Over-expression of DinI from pBAD-dinI in ΔdinI cells further confirmed this result: cells recovered storage structures in the presence of L-arabinose (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging of ΔdinI cells with inducible DinI expression.

claim: RecA* foci that co-localize with replisomes are likely associated with replisomes that are stalled at sites of DNA damage.
source: The RecA* foci that co-localize with replisomes are likely associated with replisomes that are stalled at sites of DNA damage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the co-localization data.

claim: RecA* foci that are not co-localizing with replisomes are forming in DNA gaps that are formed and left behind by the replisome.
source: We postulate that RecA* foci that are not co-localizing with replisomes are forming in DNA gaps that are formed and left behind by the replisome (Howard-Flanders et al., 1968; Rupp and Howard-Flanders, 1968; Yeeles and Marians, 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the co-localization data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Most foci of the translesion DNA polymerases IV and V also form at nucleoid locations that are distal from replisomes, both before and after SOS induction.
source: Notably, most foci of the translesion DNA polymerases IV and V also form at nucleoid locations that are distal from replisomes, both before and after SOS induction (Henrikus et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The timing of RecA bundle formation in UV experiments coincided closely with that of RecA bundles observed upon induction of site specific double-strand breaks in the chromosome.
source: Interestingly, despite the differences in the nature of the DNA damage inflicted, the timing of RecA bundle formation in our UV experiments coincided closely with that of RecA bundles observed upon induction of site specific double-strand breaks in the chromosome (Lesterlin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current data with prior work.

claim: RecA bundles may be nucleated by RecA binding to either gaps or resected double strand breaks.
source: The bundles may thus be nucleated by RecA binding to either gaps or resected double strand breaks.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed timing of bundle formation.

claim: RecA bundles also interact with anionic phospholipids in the inner membrane.
source: RecA bundles also interact with anionic phospholipids in the inner membrane (Rajendram et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: UmuC localizes primarily at the inner-membrane upon production and access to the nucleoid is regulated by the RecA* mediated UmuD cleavage.
source: Notably, UmuC also localizes primarily at the inner-membrane upon production and access to the nucleoid is regulated by the RecA* mediated UmuD cleavage (Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The GFP fluorescence in recA-gfp cells increased after DNA damage and peaked at approximately 130 min.
source: In response to UV irradiation, GFP fluorescence in recA-gfp cells increased after DNA damage and peaked at approximately 130 min (Figure 1—video 2 and Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The kinetics of the observed increase in the levels of chromosomally expressed RecA-GFP fusion protein are the same as those of the increase seen with the plasmid-based gfpmut2 reporter under control of the recA promoter.
source: Thus, the kinetics of the observed increase in the levels of chromosomally expressed RecA-GFP fusion protein are the same as those of the increase seen with the plasmid-based gfpmut2 reporter under control of the recA promoter.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from Figure 1C.

claim: Measurements of the abundance of the recA transcript after SOS induction have revealed a ten-fold increase within minutes after irradiation with UV in cells grown at 37°C upon exposure to 40 Jm−2 of UV.
source: Measurements of the abundance of the recA transcript after SOS induction have revealed a ten-fold increase within minutes after irradiation with UV in cells grown at 37°C upon exposure to 40 Jm−2 of UV (Courcelle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In bulk experiments, the amount of RecA protein has been shown to attain a maximum at 90 min after introduction of damage.
source: In bulk experiments, the amount of RecA protein has been shown to attain a maximum at 90 min after introduction of damage (Salles and Paoletti, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The recAo1403 promoter increases the basal (non-SOS) level of recA expression by a factor of 2–3.
source: The recAo1403 promoter increases the basal (non-SOS) level of recA expression by a factor of 2–3 (Rajendram et al., 2015; Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cells expressing RecA-GFP fusion protein from the recAo1403 promoter exhibit a three-fold lower survival in response to UV irradiation, and ten-fold lower ability to perform recombination.
source: Despite the higher expression level, cells expressing this RecA-GFP fusion protein are deficient in RecA functions; notably, these cells exhibit a three-fold lower survival in response to UV irradiation, and ten-fold lower ability to perform recombination (Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells expressing RecA-GFP from the recAo1403 promoter exhibit delayed kinetics of SOS induction but are still able to induce the SOS response to the same extent as wild-type cells.
source: Additionally, these cells exhibit delayed kinetics of SOS induction but are still able to induce the SOS response to the same extent as wild-type cells (Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The copy number of the SOS-reporter plasmids is not influenced by ultraviolet radiation.
source: Importantly, the copy number of these SOS-reporter plasmids is not influenced by the ultraviolet radiation (Ronen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The YPet fusion to dnaQ has been shown to minimally affect the function of ϵ.
source: The YPet fusion has previously been shown to minimally affect the function of ϵ (Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2010; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The fitness of HG267 (dnaQ-YPet/pBAD-PAmCherry-mcI) was indistinguishable from that of wild-type MG1655 at the UV doses tested in the UV-survival assay.
source: Quantification of colony forming units revealed that the fitness of HG267 was indistinguishable from that of HG116 at the doses tested in this assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on UV-survival assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only 1.5% of the lexA3(Ind-) population exhibited at least one PAmCherry-mCI focus in the absence of UV.
source: Only 1.5% of the lexA3(Ind-) (gray area Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) population exhibited at least one PAmCherry-mCI focus (compared to 19% for wild-type) (summarized in Figure 4H) in the absence of UV.
evidence: This is based on live-cell PALM imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At 60 min after UV irradiation, only 21% of the lexA3(Ind-) population exhibited PAmCherry-mCI foci compared to 56% in case of the wild-type.
source: At 60 min after UV irradiation, only 21% of the population exhibited PAmCherry-mCI foci compared to 56% in case of the wild-type (Figure 4B compare gray areas, see also 4H).
evidence: This is based on live-cell PALM imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The inability to cleave LexA results in an absence of available binding sites for PAmCherry-mCI.
source: The consistently lower number of localizations suggests that the inability to cleave LexA results in an absence of available binding sites for PAmCherry-mCI.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing lexA+ and lexA3(Ind-) cells.

claim: The non-cleavable LexA(G85D) protein competes with mCI for the same substrates in vivo.
source: This observation suggests that the non-cleavable LexA(G85D) protein competes with mCI for the same substrates in vivo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing lexA+ and lexA3(Ind-) cells.

claim: RecA* could be detected even in the absence of DNA damage in lexA+ cells.
source: Notably, RecA* could be detected even in the absence of DNA damage in lexA+ cells.
evidence: This is based on live-cell PALM imaging data.

claim: 14 ± 25% of the replisomes exhibited co-localization with mCI in lexA+ cells in the absence of UV.
source: In these cells, 14 ± 25% of the replisomes exhibited co-localization with mCI (Figure 4E, blue curve, No UV time point).
evidence: This is based on co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: RecA* filaments that are formed at sites of replisomes in the absence of UV light might reflect replication forks engaged in recombination-dependent DNA restart pathways or replication forks stalled at sites of bulky endogenous DNA damage.
source: These RecA* filaments that are formed at sites of replisomes in the absence of UV light might reflect replication forks engaged in recombination-dependent DNA restart pathways or replication forks stalled at sites of bulky endogenous DNA damage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observation of RecA* at replisomes in the absence of UV.

claim: The measured co-localization of RecA* and replisomes was significantly greater than co-localization by chance.
source: This measured co-localization was significantly greater than co-localization by chance which remained less than 1% (see Materials and methods, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of co-localization data.

claim: Some RecA* filaments are formed in cells in the vicinity of replisomes when cells are exposed to UV light.
source: These results are consistent with the model that some RecA* filaments are formed in cells in the vicinity of replisomes when cells are exposed to UV light.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the co-localization data.

claim: Most RecA* filaments appear at locations distal to the replisome.
source: Most RecA* filaments appear at locations distal to the replisome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the co-localization data showing that the majority of RecA* foci do not co-localize with replisomes.

claim: Irradiation of RecA-GFP cells with a pulse of 20 Jm−2 of UV led to the formation of large RecA structures during the SOS response.
source: Irradiation of RecA-GFP cells with a pulse of 20 Jm−2 of UV led to the formation of large RecA structures during the SOS response (Figure 5A and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RecA-GFP structures evolved from RecA foci into large cell-spanning structures.
source: These structures evolved from RecA foci into large cell-spanning structures.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: Localizations of PAmCherry-mCI resembled those of RecA-GFP in bundles at later time points after UV.
source: Examination of images of HG267 (dnaQ-YPet/pBAD-PAmCherry-mcI) cells taken at later time points revealed that localizations of PAmCherry-mCI (Figure 5B) resembled those of RecA-GFP in bundles (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of imaging data from Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: YPet-mCI initially exhibits cytosolic localization at the start of the experiment and reveals foci and bundles at later time points after UV.
source: In this experiment, YPet-mCI initially exhibits cytosolic localization at the start of the experiment (Figure 5C, t = −5 min ('No UV' time point)) and reveals foci and bundles at later time points (Figure 5C, t = 1 hr and 2 hr).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cells carrying the recA1 allele did not exhibit foci or bundles that bound to YPet-mCI after UV.
source: These cells did not exhibit foci or bundles that bound to YPet-mCI after UV (Figure 5D, strain# HG242; supplemental table 2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: mCI recognizes a specific configuration of wild-type RecA on ssDNA – one that is able to co-operatively bind and hydrolyze ATP.
source: These data demonstrate that mCI recognizes a specific configuration of wild-type RecA on ssDNA – one that is able to co-operatively bind and hydrolyze ATP.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that recA1 mutant does not support mCI binding.

claim: Cells lacking UvrD exhibited large RecA bundles and extensive cell filamentation that are hallmarks of constitutive SOS even in the absence of any external DNA damage.
source: These cells exhibited large RecA bundles and extensive cell filamentation that are hallmarks of constitutive SOS even in the absence of any external DNA damage (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In wild-type cells UvrD may play a role in disassembling persistent RecA* filaments.
source: These observations are consistent with the hypothesis that RecA* filaments are stabilized by YPet-mCI, and that in wild-type cells UvrD may play a role in disassembling persistent RecA* filaments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of large bundles in ΔuvrD cells.

claim: RecA bundles are not only formed by RecA-GFP but also by wild-type RecA during the SOS response.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that: 1) RecA bundles are not only formed by RecA-GFP but also by wild-type RecA during the SOS response
evidence: This is based on the observation that mCI stains bundles in cells expressing wild-type RecA.

claim: The ability to form RecA* – a high-affinity complex on ssDNA – is critical for the formation of RecA bundles.
source: 2) The ability to form RecA* – a high-affinity complex on ssDNA – is critical for the formation of RecA bundles.
evidence: This is based on the observation that recA1 mutant does not form bundles.

claim: RecA bundles contain an ordered assembly of RecA that is bound to DNA.
source: Further, the lack of mCI features in the recA1 background suggest that far from being DNA-free aggregates of RecA, these bundles contain an ordered assembly of RecA that is bound to DNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that mCI stains bundles and requires wild-type RecA.

claim: Cells exhibited punctate foci that appear to be positioned outside the nucleoid in the absence of DNA damage.
source: Cells exhibited punctate foci that appear to be positioned outside the nucleoid (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 2 and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figures 1D and 6A.

claim: Cells carrying RecA storage structures did not exhibit markers of distress, namely cell filamentation.
source: Notably, cells carrying these structures did not exhibit markers of distress, namely cell filamentation.
evidence: This is based on imaging observations.

claim: recA-gfp/pConst-recA cells exhibited larger features than recA-gfp/pG353C-recA cells or recA-gfp cells alone.
source: recA-gfp/pConst-recA cells exhibited larger features than recA-gfp/pG353C-recA cells or recA-gfp cells alone.
evidence: This is based on measurements of Feret diameters shown in Figure 6B.

claim: All cells exhibited storage structures, and upon cell division, the structure was inherited by one of the daughter cells.
source: All cells exhibited storage structures, and upon cell division, the structure was inherited by one of the daughter cells.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: Cells carrying the RecA over-expresser plasmid pConst-recA exhibited strong RecA staining that was localized to the membrane.
source: Cells carrying the RecA over-expresser plasmid pConst-recA exhibited strong RecA staining that was localized to the membrane (Figure 6E and F. See Figure 6—figure supplement 1B for additional examples).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: At later time points after UV, the storage structures re-appeared at locations close to the poles.
source: At later time points, the storage structures re-appeared at locations close to the poles (Figure 6G, t = 2 hr 45 min), suggesting that the RecA is stored away until needed (see also Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: In response to UV irradiation, cytosolic YPet-mCI was found to form foci and bundles.
source: However, in response to UV irradiation, cytosolic YPet-mCI was found to form foci and bundles (Figures 6I and 120 min time point; see also Figure 6—video 3).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Observations of cells expressing plasmid-based mCI in recA-gfp/pG353C-recA revealed no detectable influence of mCI on the morphology of storage structures.
source: Observations of cells expressing plasmid-based mCI in recA-gfp/pG353C-recA revealed no detectable influence of mCI on the morphology of these structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), reinforcing the interpretation that mCI does not interact with storage structures of RecA in the absence of damage.
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Upon UV irradiation, cytosolic RecA-GFP forms foci that progress to form large, cell-spanning bundles over the course of several tens of minutes.
source: Upon UV irradiation, cytosolic RecA-GFP forms foci that progress to form large, cell-spanning bundles over the course of several tens of minutes (Figure 1—video 2), unlike RecA storage structures observed in the recA-gfp/pG353C-recA cells.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: In solution, the C-terminal tail of DinI mimics ssDNA, enabling interactions with monomeric RecA.
source: In solution, the C-terminal tail of DinI mimics ssDNA, enabling interactions with monomeric RecA (Ramirez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Introduction of the single point mutation in the RBS reduced the constitutive expression of mKate2 by half.
source: We found that introduction of the single point mutation in the RBS reduced the constitutive expression of mKate2 by half (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expression of RecA from the pG353C-recA plasmid is expected to be half of that from pConst-recA in cells.
source: Based on these results, we expect the expression of RecA from the pG353C-recA plasmid to be half of that from pConst-recA in cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mKate2 expression data.

claim: A previous report on co-localization of RecA-GFP with DnaX-mCherry in Bacillus subtilis growing in minimal media reported a basal co-localization of 74.8 ± 8.4% with an increase to 84.3 ± 5.8% at 5 min after 40 Jm−2 UV treatment.
source: A previous report on co-localization of RecA-GFP with DnaX-mCherry in Bacillus subtilis growing in minimal media reported a basal co-localization of 74.8 ± 8.4% with an increase to 84.3 ± 5.8% at 5 min after 40 Jm−2 UV treatment (Lenhart et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The extent of co-localization of RecA* and replisomes detected in E. coli cells growing in media that supports multi-fork replication is lower both before and after UV irradiation compared to Bacillus subtilis.
source: The extent of co-localization of RecA* and replisomes detected in our experiments, in E. coli cells growing in media that supports multi-fork replication is lower both before and after UV irradiation.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current data with prior work in Bacillus subtilis.

claim: The copy number of the pBAD reporter plasmid has been shown to remain unchanged following ultraviolet radiation.
source: The copy number of this reporter plasmid has been shown to remain unchanged following ultraviolet radiation (Ronen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The recAo1403 operator increases the basal (non-SOS) level of recA expression by a factor of 2–3.
source: The recAo1403 promoter increases the basal (non-SOS) level of recA expression by a factor of 2–3 (Rajendram et al., 2015; Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The maturation time of gfpmut2 is less than 5 min.
source: We imaged cells that express fast-folding GFP from the gfpmut2 gene placed under the recA promoter on a low-copy reporter plasmid, with a maturation time of less than 5 min ('pRecAp-gfp' cells; strain# HG260; supplemental table 2 in Supplementary file 1) (Kalir et al., 2001; Zaslaver et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Measurements of the mean fluorescence intensity of cytosolic GFP in pRecAp-gfp cells exhibited a gradual increase peaking at approximately 135 min, with a maximum that corresponded to a two-fold increase compared to the initial fluorescence intensity.
source: Measurements of the mean fluorescence intensity of cytosolic GFP in pRecAp-gfp cells exhibited a gradual increase peaking at approximately 135 min, with a maximum that corresponded to a two-fold increase compared to the initial fluorescence intensity (Figure 1—video 1 and Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The accumulation of the fluorescent reporter protein reaches a maximum only after more than two hours after UV exposure.
source: After UV exposure, the accumulation of the fluorescent reporter protein reaches a maximum only after more than two hours.
evidence: This is based on the observation that fluorescence peaks at approximately 135 min.

claim: The gradual increase in fluorescence is used to define the time period during which cellular RecA concentration is increasing after UV treatment.
source: By extension, this gradual increase is used here to define the time period during which cellular RecA concentration is increasing after UV treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence data.

claim: The increase in recA gene expression counters the dilution in the cellular RecA concentration that is caused by the filamentation of the cells.
source: The increase in recA gene expression counters the dilution in the cellular RecA concentration that is caused by the filamentation of the cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increase in RecA expression during cell filamentation.

claim: During the SOS response, many cells undergo filamentation as cell division is blocked while some DNA synthesis continues.
source: During the SOS response, many cells undergo filamentation as cell division is blocked while some DNA synthesis continues (Howard-Flanders et al., 1968).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Damage in the template strand can result in the stalling or decoupling of replication, leading to the accumulation of single-stranded DNA.
source: Damage in the template strand can result in the stalling or decoupling of replication, leading to the accumulation of single-stranded DNA.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the Results section.

claim: This ssDNA provides a RecA nucleation site to form RecA*, the structure that amplifies the cellular signal for genetic instability.
source: This ssDNA provides a RecA nucleation site to form RecA*, the structure that amplifies the cellular signal for genetic instability (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Production of RecA occurs rapidly after damage.
source: Because production of RecA occurs rapidly after damage, it is critical to observe live cells at early time points with high temporal resolution after SOS induction.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: RecA and related recombinases are highly regulated, with a variety of accessory proteins governing every facet of their multiple functions.
source: Unsurprisingly, RecA and related recombinases are highly regulated, with a variety of accessory proteins governing every facet of their multiple functions (Cox, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Directed-evolution approaches can be used to enhance the catalytic activities of recombinases in cells.
source: Directed-evolution approaches can be used to enhance the catalytic activities of recombinases in cells (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RecA functional enhancement has a cost, disrupting an evolved balance between the various processes of DNA metabolism that share a common genomic DNA substrate.
source: However, RecA functional enhancement has a cost, disrupting an evolved balance between the various processes of DNA metabolism that share a common genomic DNA substrate (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Many deleterious genomic events occur at the interfaces between replication, repair, recombination, and transcription.
source: Many deleterious genomic events occur at the interfaces between replication, repair, recombination, and transcription.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The properties of RecA assemblies are often determined by the state of hydrolysis of associated ATP.
source: The properties of these assemblies are often determined by the state of hydrolysis of associated ATP.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: EM studies of RecA-ssDNA filaments have revealed that the pitch of the filament depends on the co-factor bound to it.
source: EM studies of RecA-ssDNA filaments have revealed that the pitch of the filament depends on the co-factor bound to it (Egelman and Stasiak, 1986; Egelman and Stasiak, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ATPγS promotes the formation of the extended filament, whereas, the ADP bound filament exhibits the compressed state.
source: Notably, ATPγS promotes the formation of the extended filament, whereas, the ADP bound filament exhibits the compressed state.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge based on prior EM studies.

claim: ATPγS traps the RecA filament in an 'active' conformation that is capable of LexA repressor autocatalytic cleavage.
source: Since ATPγS traps the RecA filament in an 'active' conformation that is capable of LexA repressor autocatalytic cleavage, we interpreted the 0.2 FRET state as corresponding to the active state (Craig and Roberts, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: One mCI contacts two RecA monomers.
source: Based on previous findings that one mCI contacts two RecA monomers, we estimate that up to six mCI molecules can decorate the RecA-ssDNA filament composed of up to 13 RecA monomers on the dT40 DNA substrate under conditions of saturating mCI concentration (Galkin et al., 2009; Ndjonka and Bell, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Up to six mCI molecules can decorate the RecA-ssDNA filament composed of up to 13 RecA monomers on the dT40 DNA substrate under conditions of saturating mCI concentration.
source: Based on previous findings that one mCI contacts two RecA monomers, we estimate that up to six mCI molecules can decorate the RecA-ssDNA filament composed of up to 13 RecA monomers on the dT40 DNA substrate under conditions of saturating mCI concentration (Galkin et al., 2009; Ndjonka and Bell, 2006).
evidence: This is an estimate based on prior structural studies and the length of the DNA substrate.

claim: Both mCI and LexA interact in the groove of the RecA* filament.
source: Current models based on EM reconstructions suggest that both mCI and LexA interact in the groove of the RecA* filament (Galkin et al., 2009; Ndjonka and Bell, 2006; Yu and Egelman, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RecA* occupies a central role in homologous recombination (HR) where it executes the homology search and strand-exchange required for HR.
source: RecA* occupies a central role in homologous recombination (HR) where it executes the homology search and strand-exchange required for HR.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: μM concentrations (2–10 μM) of mCI potently inhibited strand exchange.
source: We found that μM concentrations (2–10 μM) of mCI potently inhibited strand exchange (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on in vitro strand exchange assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Tagged mCI constructs did not significantly inhibit strand-exchange activity at concentrations below 500 nM.
source: Importantly, tagged mCI constructs did not significantly inhibit strand-exchange activity at concentrations below 500 nM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on in vitro strand exchange assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Incubation of pre-formed RecA* filaments on circular ssDNA M13mp18 substrates with micromolar concentrations of mCI revealed a pronounced inhibition of RecA* ATPase activity.
source: Incubation of pre-formed RecA* filaments on circular ssDNA M13mp18 substrates with micromolar concentrations of mCI revealed a pronounced inhibition of RecA* ATPase activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on in vitro ATPase assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The tagged mCI variants did not significantly inhibit RecA* ATPase activity at concentrations under 500 nM.
source: The tagged mCI variants did not significantly inhibit RecA* ATPase activity at concentrations under 500 nM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on in vitro ATPase assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Even high concentrations of mCI did not inhibit LexA cleavage.
source: Quantification of the percentage of uncleaved LexA as a function of time revealed that even high concentrations of mCI did not inhibit LexA cleavage.
evidence: This is based on in vitro LexA cleavage assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: μM concentrations of mCI induced a delay in the kinetics of LexA cleavage.
source: However, μM concentrations of mCI induced a delay in the kinetics of LexA cleavage.
evidence: This is based on in vitro LexA cleavage assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: At low levels of L-arabinose supplementation (<10−3%), cells exhibit SOS induction levels that are comparable to wild-type cells.
source: At low levels of L-arabinose supplementation (<10−3%), cells exhibit SOS induction levels that are comparable to wild-type cells.
evidence: This is based on live-cell imaging experiments measuring SOS reporter fluorescence.

claim: Despite the weaker affinity of tagged mCI to RecA* compared to untagged mCI, their effects on SOS induction in cells were comparable.
source: Notably, despite the weaker affinity of tagged mCI to RecA* compared to untagged mCI, their effects on SOS induction in cells were comparable.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SOS induction data for cells expressing mCI vs. PAmCherry-mCI.

claim: The leading model for SOS induction is that replication forks fail at sites of lesions and produce large tracts of ssDNA that templates nucleation of RecA filaments.
source: The leading model for SOS induction is that replication forks fail at sites of lesions and produce large tracts of ssDNA that templates nucleation of RecA filaments.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The two-color strain was grown in medium containing small amounts of L-arabinose (5 × 10−4%%) to induce low expression of PAmCherry-mCI in the 10–100 nM concentration range in cells.
source: The two-color strain was grown in medium containing small amounts of L-arabinose (5 × 10−4%%) to induce low expression of PAmCherry-mCI in the 10–100 nM concentration range in cells.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: lexA3(Ind-) cells did not exhibit PAmCherry-mCI foci that co-localized with replisomes before UV irradiation.
source: Strikingly, lexA3(Ind-) cells did not exhibit PAmCherry-mCI foci that co-localized with replisomes before UV irradiation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: At 60 min after UV, 32 ± 11% of the PAmCherry-mCI foci co-localized with replisomes in lexA3(Ind-) cells.
source: At 60 min, 32 ± 11% of the PAmCherry-mCI foci co-localized with replisomes (Figure 4F and H).
evidence: This is based on co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The number of replisome foci detected per cell ranged from 3.5 ± 1.4 (mean ± standard deviation) in the absence of UV to 4.2 ± 2.1 per cell at t = 60 min after UV.
source: The number of replisome foci detected per cell was found to remain relatively constant ranging from 3.5 ± 1.4 (mean ± standard deviation) in the absence of UV to 4.2 ± 2.1 per cell at t = 60 min after UV (blue line, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The number of PAmCherry-mCI foci marking sites of RecA* increased approximately five-fold from 0.3 ± 0.6 per cell before UV irradiation to 1.4 ± 0.25 per cell at t = 60 min.
source: The number of PAmCherry-mCI foci marking sites of RecA* was found to increase approximately five-fold from 0.3 ± 0.6 per cell before UV irradiation to 1.4 ± 0.25 per cell at t = 60 min (red line, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Among cells exhibiting at least one focus, 24 ± 37% (mean ± standard deviation) of PAmCherry-mCI foci co-localized with replisomes before UV irradiation, and this number increased to 34 ± 37% at 60 min after UV.
source: Among cells exhibiting at least one focus (gray area), 24 ± 37% (mean ± standard deviation) of PAmCherry-mCI foci co-localized with replisomes before UV irradiation, and this number increased to 34 ± 37% at 60 min after UV (Figure 4D and H).
evidence: This is based on co-localization analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The number of PAmCherry-mCI foci detected in lexA3(Ind-) cells remained consistently low, starting at 0.03 ± 0.25 (mean ± standard deviation) prior to UV irradiation and reaching a value of 0.3 ± 0.7 foci per cell at 60 min.
source: Quantification of the number of foci per cell revealed that the number of PAmCherry-mCI foci detected remained consistently low, starting at 0.03 ± 0.25 (mean ± standard deviation) prior to UV irradiation and reaching a value of 0.3 ± 0.7 foci per cell at 60 min (compare red lines in Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: In the absence of UV, 19% of all lexA+ cells exhibited at least one PAmCherry-mCI focus.
source: In the absence of DNA damage, 19% of all lexA+ cells exhibited at least one PAmCherry-mCI focus (Figure 4A and B (lexA+ panel, gray shaded area), t = −5 min; summarized in Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In response to UV damage, the number of lexA+ cells with at least one PAmCherry focus increased to 56% of the population at t = 60 min after UV.
source: In response to UV damage inflicted at t = 0 min, we detected an increase in the number of lexA+ cells with at least one PAmCherry focus to 56% of the population at t = 60 min after UV (Figure 4B, total numbers for each time point are presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In this L-arabinose concentration regime, the mCI copy number is expected to be approximately 20, 50 and 500 copies per cell for 0, 10−3 or 10−2% L-arabinose, respectively.
source: In this L-arabinose concentration regime, we expect the mCI copy number to be approximately 20, 50 and 500 copies per cell, respectively (Ghodke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an estimate based on a citation to prior work.

claim: mCI competes with LexA in cells at sites of RecA* in response to DNA damage.
source: These data suggest that mCI competes with LexA in cells at sites of RecA* in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the SOS inhibition data.

claim: The copy number of pConst-recA is expected to be approximately six copies per cell.
source: pConst-recA has a pSC101 origin of replication and its copy number is expected to be approximately six copies per cell (Cabello et al., 1976; Hasunuma and Sekiguchi, 1977; Peterson and Phillips, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the RBS strongly influence the complementarity to the 16S rRNA and consequently influence the efficiency of translation.
source: Since mutations in the RBS strongly influence the complementarity to the 16S rRNA and consequently influence the efficiency of translation, we anticipated that this G to C transversion would reduce the expression level from the strong recA RBS (Johnson et al., 1991; Shine and Dalgarno, 1974; Shine and Dalgarno, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cells carrying pConst-mKate2 exhibit two-fold higher mKate2 fluorescence on average than cells expressing mKate2 from the RBS mutant (G353C) of the recAo281 promoter.
source: Cells carrying the constitutive RecA promoter (recAo281) exhibit two-fold higher mKate2 fluorescence on average (mean ± standard deviation = 13298 ± 4085 arb. units) than cells expressing mKate2 from the RBS mutant (G353C) of the recAo281 promoter (6879 ± 2150 arb. units).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The recA1 allele is an inactive mutant (G160D).
source: To that end, we imaged YPet-mCI in cells carrying the recA1 allele (an inactive mutant, G160D) (Bryant, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The recA1 allele fails to support focus or bundle formation.
source: These cells did not exhibit foci or bundles that bound to YPet-mCI after UV (Figure 5D, strain# HG242; supplemental table 2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The recA1 allele is unable to induce SOS and HR functions.
source: The recA1 allele failed to support focus or bundle formation, consistent with the inability of the RecA(G160D) to induce SOS and HR functions (Bryant, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells lacking UvrD have been shown to exhibit large foci formed by the RecA(R28A)-GFP mutant that does not form DNA-free aggregates.
source: Cells lacking UvrD have been shown to exhibit large foci formed by the RecA(R28A)-GFP mutant that does not form DNA-free aggregates (Centore and Sandler, 2007; Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: UvrD disassembles RecA filaments in cells.
source: We investigated whether RecA bundles decorated by mCI are modulated by the UvrD helicase that disassembles RecA filaments in cells (Centore and Sandler, 2007; Lestini and Michel, 2007; Petrova et al., 2015; Veaute et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: UvrD limits RecA filament formation both in vitro and in vivo.
source: These observations are qualitatively consistent with previous findings that UvrD limits RecA filament formation both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as consistent with prior findings.

claim: The R28A mutant of RecA exhibits fewer foci in cells when tagged to GFP.
source: RecA forms DNA-free aggregates in vitro, and the R28A mutant of RecA exhibits fewer foci in cells when tagged to GFP (Eldin et al., 2000; Renzette et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The DinI protein is a modulator of RecA function.
source: The DinI protein is a modulator of RecA function (Lusetti et al., 2004a; Lusetti et al., 2004b; Renzette et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ordered assemblies of RecA have been previously detected in cells after nalidixic acid treatment.
source: Ordered assembles of RecA have been previously detected in cells after nalidixic acid treatment (Levin-Zaidman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RecA bundles are similar to RecA structures called 'threads', that nucleate at engineered double-strand breaks in Bacillus subtilis.
source: These bundles are similar to RecA structures called 'threads', that nucleate at engineered double-strand breaks in Bacillus subtilis (Kidane and Graumann, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The appearance of elongated RecA* foci after treatment with ultraviolet (UV) radiation has not always been associated with bundle formation.
source: The appearance of elongated RecA* foci after treatment with ultraviolet (UV) radiation has not always been associated with bundle formation (Renzette et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.
